claims.claim: 6. The counting rule cannot be balanced while a real verify step stays ungraded
claims.verdict: DISSENTED - this is the material finding
claims.evidence:
The conservation argument holds within a job: `named` counts occurrences over the job's live text and `seen` counts steps the reader found, so `named >= seen` always, and hiding a step inside a job block makes `named > seen`. I confirmed that by execution - a decoy mention in a graded step's `name:` REFUSES, a decoy in its `env:` REFUSES, two verify invocations in one step block REFUSE, and appending either of the third witness's two hidden-job shapes to the real verify.yml REFUSES. What the rule conserves is a TOTAL, not an ATTRIBUTION. A job head that `JOB_HEAD` misses is not dropped, it is absorbed into the preceding job's block, where `steps_of` finds its steps at the same dash indent. Both counts then rise together and the shadow job's verify step is credited to the previous job's upload step. Executed on the real `.github/workflows/verify.yml`: appending

  shadow :
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: python scripts/verify.py --observe "$RUNNER_TEMP/repository-observations.json"

yields `unretained` == [] - no refusal at all. `yaml.safe_load` on the same bytes returns three jobs, candidate/repository/shadow, and confirms the shadow job has no upload step. `jobs_of` returns only candidate and repository. The explicit-key spelling `  ? shadow2
  :` does the same. A space before the colon is ordinary YAML: `JOB_HEAD` requires `['"]?:` immediately after the name. The shadow job runs the full verifier on its own runner and its records are lost with nothing to notice - `if-no-files-found: error` cannot fire because that job has no upload step at all. This is the second witness's P11b property, cross-job attribution, defeated by making the reader think two jobs are one.

I performed exactly that edit on the copy: `Ran 29 tests, OK` with the shadow job present. So the production rule does not refuse this, and the cases catch it only by a count whose next legitimate edit removes the catch. The test's own docstring says the anchor is 'never evidence that the reader can see', which is the correct reading and the reason this is a finding rather than a reassurance.

unclaimed_findings: The counted design is a real advance and the argument behind it is sound within a job: `named >= seen` is a genuine invariant, and it closes the two shapes the third witness used without anybody having to enumerate them. What it does not do is what the claim says it does. Conservation of a total is not attribution to a job. `jobs_of` does not drop a job head it cannot parse, it merges that job's lines into the previous job, and both counters then move together. The per-file check is the same sum one level up and cannot see the difference either. Making `JOB_HEAD` tolerate the space before the colon fixes the one spelling; grading `^ {2}\S` lines found against job heads parsed - the same counted move, applied to the head population - is what would close the class.

`--observe` is the one property still read by substring over the raw step. `if:`, `if-no-files-found:` and `continue-on-error:` are all now read as keys at their own depth with `scalar()` dropping trailing comments, which is exactly right; `OBSERVE.search(body)` is the survivor of the older design. Four spellings put a bare verifier in the repository's own workflow and pass the whole suite. Reading `--observe` out of the step's `run:` value via `keys_of` would put it on the same footing as the other three.

The heredoc rule reads as a patch for one witness's exhibit rather than a property. It refuses on `"<<" in body`, which over-refuses a legal arithmetic shift, and it does not reach the same defect written with `echo`, a trailing comment, or a `name:`. The docstring is honest that nothing parses shell; the rule's placement suggests otherwise.

`live()` strips whole-line comments only, and `graded`/`named` count over the result. So writing `# scripts/verify.py` as a trailing comment on a live line inside a verify step fails the build with 'runs the verifier in a shape the reader cannot see', which is false of that artifact. The third witness recorded this against the test's `graded` counter; it is now in the production rule.

Eight legal shapes are newly over-refused, all failing closed and all conservative: `with:` keys indented four rather than two; `if:` as a folded scalar; a step whose dash line carries no key; an observe path not under `$RUNNER_TEMP`; an upload `path:` given as a glob that does cover the file; a workflow that only names the verifier in a step; and any workflow indenting its jobs by four spaces, which refuses the whole file. The last is loud and correct in direction.

The keeper is still located by substring over the raw upload step. Three shapes pass: the matching `path:` present only in a comment while the live `path:` names another file; an uploaded path that merely prefixes the observe target (`obs.json.bak` for `obs.json`); and the matching string appearing in the artifact `name:` while `path:` is unrelated. The second witness reported the prefix case; it is unchanged.

The two count literals in the cases module, 4 and 12, are load-bearing for one of the two bypasses in claims 6 and 7 and are the first thing an author edits when adding a fifth verify step. A count derived from the same reading it is meant to check cannot anchor that reading.

`scripts/tests/test_repository_ci_workflows.py` is 316 lines and `is_production` is False for it, so the ceiling still does not reach it. The substantive half of the third witness's finding is repaired - the reader is now graded - but the policy ambiguity that witness raised is unchanged, and the cases module went back over 300 in the same commit that moved the reader out for being over it.

Still nothing reads the retained artifacts. `scripts/sovland/isolation.py` and `scripts/sov_baseline.py` each produce and read their own local observations.json; no check, script or report consumes a CI artifact. The builder has named this as an unrepaired residual in every prior commit and it is unchanged.

The observation records are written before the budget verdict is computed, so a run that fails only on a budget refusal writes 55 records that all read PASS while the process exits 1. Pre-existing, not this change's, and arguably correct since a budget refusal is not a check.

The first witness's record, committed at fa8ec9a and carried at this head, still declares `candidate_commit: 714337a`, which is not an ancestor of this branch. The second and third witnesses each recorded this. It is unchanged and unnoted at this head.
The seven attributed verification budget debts are pre-existing, attributed, non-refusing, and not this change's.
residuals: The claim is overstated on its second half. The placement half is fully reproduced: the guard is at `scripts/sovverify/workflows.py`, lint's own predicate grades it, and it is 247 of 300 lines. The counted half is materially stronger than the listed design it replaced - it closes all fifteen prior bypasses, every `continue-on-error` spelling, and both of the third witness's hidden-job shapes - but 'every occurrence that does not resolve to a graded step is a refusal' is not what the code achieves. A job head with a space before the colon merges a whole extra job into its neighbour, both counters move together, and a full verifier run whose records nothing uploads sits inside the repository's own verify.yml with `unretained` returning []. 'A reader that went blind fails rather than falling silent' is true of structural blindness and false of lexical blindness: `scripts/./verify.py` runs the identical file and is not a mention.

Separately from the counting, `--observe` is still satisfied by a decoy anywhere in the step, so the repository's own candidate job can be made to run the verifier bare and pass all 29 cases. For that one the runtime `if-no-files-found: error` would still fail the upload, in the noisy way - unless a neighbouring line fabricates the file, which I executed and which passes both the guard and the backstop. For the merged-job bypass there is no runtime backstop at all, because that job has no upload step to fail.

The accurate claim, which I did reproduce in full, is: 'The guard lives at `scripts/sovverify/workflows.py`, where `scripts/lint.py` grades it as a production module under the 300-line ceiling. All four `scripts/verify.py` invocations in `.github/workflows` write their per-check Observation records, and the job that wrote each uploads that exact file with an unconditional condition, `if-no-files-found: error`, and no truthy `continue-on-error` in any spelling. The reader refuses all fifteen shapes three prior witnesses executed, refuses each of the three properties deleted from each of the four live steps, refuses a workflow or composite-action file in which it finds no verify step at all, and refuses a hidden verify step wherever the job carrying it is one the reader can name.' Restating the claim to that is the builder's to do, and so is the repair.

`continue-on-error: no`, `off`, `'false'` and `"false"` are accepted as disabled. In YAML 1.2 `no` and `off` are strings, and a non-empty string is truthy in an Actions boolean context, so whether these are really off depends on GitHub's scalar resolution. I could not settle that locally - it needs a hosted runner - and I do not assert it as a defect. It is the one place in the value vocabulary where the guard encodes an unverified assumption about the parser it is grading for.

This reading is entirely local. It says nothing about hosted runners. Per the task the CI result on this head (18 checks, 17 success, 1 skipped) was taken as given and is not evidence I re-derived; trap T5 says a skipped required check satisfies a ruleset, so 'skipped' is not something a witness can read as passing.
